kraal.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *ḱers-
Proto-Indo-European *-ós
Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós
Proto-Italic *korzos
Vulgar Latin currus
Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-
Proto-Indo-European *-is
Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.?
Proto-Italic *-ālis
Vulgar Latin -ālis
Vulgar Latin *currālis?
Old Galician-Portuguese curral
Portuguese curralbor.
Dutch kraalbor.
English kraal
From colonial Dutch kraal, from Portuguese curral. Doublet of corral.

s.d: a village of huts for native Africans in southern Africa; usually surrounded by a stockade
a pen for livestock in southern Africa
In Central and Southern Africa, a small rural community.
x: Onanis is the permanent residence of a kraal of very poor Hill-Damaras, who subsist chiefly upon the few wild roots which their sterile neighborhood produces.
‘The paraffin box covered with newsprint, and the primus, and the bucket standing on the floor, and a photo of our kraal’s chief on the wall.’

s.d: An enclosure for livestock.
x: The animal, which is now six years old, was born naturally from the mating of a female goat with a male sheep sharing the same kraal.

s.d: To enclose (livestock) within a kraal or stockade.
x: […] he knew that one of these beasts was in the habit of harassing the goat-kids, which, for better security, he had kraaled against the wall of the house.

kraft.e: Borrowed from Swedish kraft (“strength”) as used in kraftpapper. Doublet of craft.

s.d: strong wrapping paper made from pulp processed with a sulfur solution
(uncountable) A kind of strong, smooth brown wrapping paper.
strong wrapping paper made from pulp processed with a sulfur solution
(uncountable) Strong paper made from kraft pulp, often used for making corrugated board; usually brown.

krait.e: Borrowed from Hindi करैत (karait), possibly from Kurux, a Dravidian language.

s.d: brightly colored venomous but nonaggressive snake of southeastern Asia and Malay peninsula
Any of several brightly-coloured, venomous snakes, of the genus Bungarus, of southeast Asia.
x: On visiting the General Hospital, on the morning of the 22nd of August, I was informed that one of the punkah coolies had been bitten about 8.30 p.m., the night before, by a krait, whose venom is virulently poisonous.
Now, if you run into one of these kraits, you better NOT run away else you're a goner. It'll catch you for sure and you will die in your tracks.

s.d: atrophy and shriveling of the skin or mucous membrane
A condition of the genitals characterized by atrophy and shriveling of the skin or mucous membranes.
x: I believe, as mentioned by Dr. Tyrone, that in leukoplakic conditions, krauroses and other chronic lesions of the vulva, simple vulvectomy will afford practically 100 per cent prophylaxis against carcinoma.

s.d: kraurosis of the vulva; often a precancerous lesion
(uncountable) A cutaneous condition characterized by atrophy and shrinkage of the skin of the vagina and vulva, often accompanied by a chronic inflammatory reaction in the deeper tissues.

kremlin.e: Similar forms are attested, per Vasmer's Etymological Dictionary, in earlier German Kremelin and French Cremlin, which are theorized to come from Old East Slavic кремльнъ (kremlĭnŭ, “having a kremlin”), from кремль (kremlĭ), whence Russian кремль (kremlʹ).

s.d: citadel of a Russian town
A fortified, central complex found in various Russian cities.
x: 9% of historical parks are the gardens of monasteries and kremlins (fortified centres in the towns), 8% are urban ("public") gardens and only 2% are parks on urban estates.
Several cities in Russia were built around fortresses called kremlins. Russians built kremlins for defense during the Middle Ages. A kremlin was often located along a river.

krennerite.e: From Krenner + -ite, after mineralogist Joseph Krenner who discovered it.

s.d: an orthorhombic gold telluride mineral which can contain a relatively small amount of silver in the structure.
x: Both of the chemically similar gold-silver tellurides, calaverite and sylvanite, are in the monoclinic crystal system, whereas krennerite is orthorhombic.

s.d: An orthorhombic-pyramidal creamy white mineral containing gold and tellurium.
any small branched yellow-flowered North American herb of the genus Krigia
Any plant of the genus Krigia.
x: Krigias are a small group of native composites, little known to gardeners.

s.d: shrimp-like planktonic crustaceans; major source of food for e.g. baleen whales
Any of several small marine crustacean species of plankton in the order Euphausiacea in the class Malacostraca.
x: “This science relates to krill and krill ecosystems, whale acoustic monitoring and Southern Ocean ecosystems,” the spokesperson said.

s.d: (slang) Crack cocaine.
x: Instead she wanna hear the beatbox / Take pills and make fake krills as sheetrock

kris.e: Borrowed from Malay keris. Doublet of kalis. Recognized as part of English ca. 1580.

s.d: a Malayan dagger with a wavy blade
A traditional Indonesian, Malaysian, or Filipino sword or dagger having a tapering, usually serpentine blade.
x: Anne Talbot looked demurely ravishing, as was her intention, in a very low-cut evening frock of bottle-green, choker of Kelantan silver, earrings in the shape of krises.

s.d: To stab or cut with a kris; to kill with a kris.
x: [...] when I was a boy, but Rajah Sul and Sultan Abdel krissed and speared all the poor people and burned the campongs.
One Malay seaman had resisted the rattan halter––he had been krissed to death on the spot and thrown overboard.

krona.e: Borrowed from Swedish krona (“crown”). Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, króna, and krone.

s.d: the basic unit of money in Sweden
the basic unit of money in Iceland
The official currency of Sweden.

krone.e: From Danish krone (“crown”) and Norwegian krone. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, krona, and króna.

s.d: the basic unit of money in Norway
the basic unit of money in Denmark
The currency of Iceland, Denmark (including Greenland and the Faroe Islands) and Norway, divided into 100 øre, except in Iceland where 1 króna = 100 aurar.

(historical) The currency of German-Austria and Liechtenstein after the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire (1919) until the introduction of the Austrian schilling and, in Liechtenstein, the Swiss franc.

kroon.e:
Etymology tree
Low German krōneder.
Estonian kroonbor.
English kroon
From Estonian kroon (“crown”). Doublet of crown and corona.

s.d: the basic unit of money in Estonia
The former currency of Estonia, divided into 100 senti.
malodorous tropical plant having a spathe that resembles the corolla of a morning glory and attains a diameter of several feet
(uncountable) The plant Amorphophallus titanum, the titan arum.

krummhorn.e: From German Krummhorn, from krumm (“crooked”) + Horn (“horn”). Doublet of cromorna.

s.d: a Renaissance woodwind with a double reed and a curving tube (crooked horn)
A mediaeval and Renaissance wind instrument.
A stop on an organ.

krypton.e:
Etymology tree
Ancient Greek κρῠ́πτω (krŭ́ptō)
Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós)
Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃-der.?
Latin carbōnemlbor.
French carbonebor.
English carbonbf.
English -on
English krypton
From Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”) + -on, used for all noble gases.

s.d: a colorless element that is one of the six inert gasses; occurs in trace amounts in air

(uncountable) The chemical element (symbol Kr) with an atomic number of 36. It is a colourless, odourless noble gas that only reacts with fluorine. It is one of the rarest gases in the Earth's atmosphere.
An atom of this element.
